canberra.title: Check your mailboxes, Canberra. You too might have a speeding fine from 19 years ago!
canberra.snippet: A Canberra man has been left shocked and confused after opening a letter with a couple of speeding fines dated all the way back to 2007. ...
canberra.content:
Canberra man Robert Scott has been issued two fines for speeding on Canberra Avenue. The strange part is that they both occurred 19 years ago. Photo: Robert Scott.

A Canberra man has been left shocked and confused after opening a letter with a couple of speeding fines dated all the way back to 2007.

Robert Scott was opening his mail on Monday evening when he came across infringement notices that showed the registration details of a car he hasn’t driven for over a decade.

Mr Scott ran outside to double-check his vehicles, believing it to be a mistake.

Once back inside, he soon realised that the infringements were dated May and June 2007.

“I’ve got no idea how it happened because if I haven’t paid a fine for the last 20 years, I would have a suspended licence,” he said.

“I don’t understand how I didn’t receive a fine back then. I don’t understand how there haven’t been updates since, and I don’t understand how I’m now receiving a reminder nearly 20 years later.”

When Mr Scott contacted Access Canberra, he was told he was issued the fine in 2007; however, he insists he has no recollection of receiving a letter.

“I was in my 20s. I was in between living at my girlfriend’s place and my parents’ place. So I’ve got no recollection of the fines from 20 years ago,” he said.

“Since 2007, I have registered several cars many times. At no point was I flagged for demerit points or told that there were any outstanding fines.

“The only time I’ve even been pulled up by police in that time was earlier this year. I didn’t do anything wrong; it was just being pulled over for a check, but they didn’t flag anything then either.”

He also said he found it ironic that, despite the near two-decade-long gap, he has only 28 days to pay the fines or set up a payment plan.

Mr Scott is not the only one to have received a fine from the ACT Government with lengthy periods between the infringement and the issuing of notices.

Several interstate residents have also been hit with new fines for old offences, with examples being shared from 2018, 2012 and 2009.

A Northern Territory resident, who was issued a fine in late August, said his offence occurred in 2012, with the notice stating he drove 72 km/h in a 60 zone on Canberra Avenue, the same place Mr Scott was pinged on in 2007.

According to Road Transport (Offences) Regulation 2005, “The administering authority must serve the infringement notice on the nominated person as soon as practicable, but not later than 1 year after the authority accepts the infringement notice declaration”.

Mr Scott said he is willing to contest the two fines but is unsure whether anything will amount from it. He believes the fines issued must have come from administrative error.

“I think it’s more likely there are bugs in their system that they haven’t ironed out over the last 20 years,” he said.

“If it’s a person, then there has to be an administrative error that has occurred. If it’s a computer, I don’t understand why they are looking over files from nearly 20 years ago.

“Even looking over the infringement notice, there’s no picture attached to either of them proving that I was going over the limit in either case.”

The total of both fines is $327. Mr Scott said he is unsure whether that is in 2007 or 2026 dollars.

Region has reached out to Access Canberra for comment on its infringement notice policy, potential statutes of limitations and whether it is actively tracking older offences.

canberra.title: Driver crashes into police car while allegedly fleeing officers
canberra.snippet: Officers tried to stop a car before its driver allegedly drove dangerously and crashed into a police vehicle in northern Canberra. An ACT...
canberra.content:
9 September 2026

Benjamin Connor Quirk-Buckley, 23, has been remanded in custody on driving charges. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Officers tried to stop a car before its driver allegedly drove dangerously and crashed into a police vehicle in northern Canberra.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said officers were patrolling Athllon Drive in Phillip on Sunday (6 September) when they spotted two speeding vehicles, including a white Kia Cerato.

Officers activated their emergency lights and sirens and directed the cars to stop, but the drivers fled the area.

Officers were then driving along Northbourne Avenue in Lyneham on Tuesday afternoon (8 September) when they saw the same Kia Cerato.

When they turned on their lights and sirens, the driver allegedly sped off, drove through a red traffic light and started driving along the Federal Highway.

But the police spokesperson said the Cerato then crashed into an unmarked police vehicle and a street sign near the highway’s intersection with Flemington Road.

Four people got out of the crashed car before the alleged driver tried to flee the scene.

“After climbing a barbed wire fence and a short foot pursuit, he was arrested by police and transported to the ACT Watch House,” the police spokesperson said.

Officers also allegedly found one passenger had a set of knuckle dusters.

The alleged driver, 23-year-old Benjamin Connor Quirk-Buckley of Richardson, was charged with furious driving, failing to stop for police and unlicensed driving.

It is alleged he has never held a licence.

His lawyer, Niamh Dwyer of Legal Aid, said he would not apply for bail when he faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Wednesday (9 September).

Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson remanded Quirk-Buckley in custody and adjourned the matter to a future date.

The passenger, a 20-year-old man, was charged with possessing an offensive weapon and was also scheduled to face the court.

canberra.title: Public service bosses don’t want their committee evidence popping up on social media
canberra.snippet: Senior public servants are arcing up about the way politicians are using their parliamentary committee appearances on social media – and ...
canberra.content:
Celia Perkins said she and her colleagues “do not consent to the reposting of our evidence to social media sites or the reproduction of our likenesses for purposes outside the framework of the parliament”. Image: Screenshot.

Senior public servants are arcing up about the way politicians are using their parliamentary committee appearances on social media – and things could get ugly.

They have already come close, with a senior Defence Department official being immediately castigated for telling a public inquiry that senators on that committee had no right to post her evidence on social media.

Top bureaucrats regularly appear before Senate Estimates and other committee inquiries held by both houses of parliament to answer questions on policy delivery and their interactions with government.

In recent years, however, some exchanges between the officials and the elected representatives sitting on committee panels have at times strayed into personal accusations and badgering.

Some senators and MPs have been accused of using bullying tactics in how they pursue lines of questioning.

While that debate is ongoing, public servants have added another grievance, and it has to do with how they are portrayed on social media.

This first became apparent in a recent committee appearance by Defence Deputy Secretary Celia Perkins.

In giving evidence before the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, Ms Perkins said she and her colleagues appearing as witnesses “do not consent to the reposting of our evidence to social media sites or the reproduction of our likenesses for purposes outside the framework of the parliament”.

Greens senator David Shoebridge immediately described it as an “extraordinary proposal” and reminded Ms Perkins that it was a public hearing and she and her colleagues are paid with taxpayers’ money.

“I’m going to make it very clear that where there’s evidence from any of these Defence officials that I think is relevant to share with the broader public, I will do so and I won’t be silenced in doing that by a Defence official,” he said.

“This is evidence given in an open public hearing … these witnesses … do not get to censor what the Australian public sees.”

Senator Shoebridge then called for a short adjournment for the committee to seek advice from the Senate Clerk over the matter.

After the break, committee chair Liberal senator Jessica Collins told the witnesses the advice was that committee members could disseminate evidence in any manner they see fit.

No prizes for guessing what footage subsequently featured on the Greens’ social media posts.

The Secretaries Board, representing department heads across the Australian Public Service, has taken up the issue with the Joint Committee on Parliamentary Standards.

It has written to the committee, raising concerns about bullying of public officials giving evidence, as well as how evidence is used on social media.

“The board’s concern is not robust questioning itself. Strong scrutiny is both legitimate and necessary,” its submission states.

“The concern arises only where conduct crosses the line into behaviour that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets official witnesses.

“The board is also concerned about the increasing use of excerpts from committee proceedings on social media, particularly where material is presented without context and exposes officials to ridicule, hostility or abuse.”

The Secretaries Board noted that parliamentarians, political offices and third parties can readily extract short segments of committee broadcasts and distribute them to large audiences via social media.

“While committee proceedings are public, and transparency is a fundamental feature of parliamentary accountability, concerns arise where excerpts:

  • present an incomplete or misleading representation of exchanges
  • remove questions or answers from their broader context
  • portray public servants as personally responsible for government policy decisions
  • invite ridicule, hostility or abuse directed at individual officials, or
  • generate significant online harassment and abuse directed toward witnesses and their families, including behaviour that is threatening or intimidating.

“The posting of videos raises an additional matter of concern, particularly where these videos are edited to exclude parts of an exchange and/or add closed captions with highlights or additional commentary.”

The board’s submission says social media posts often attract offensive and threatening messages from public users directed at officials.

It has called for guidelines for MPs, including a ban on selectively editing evidence clips.

Not everyone is ignoring their complaints. Labor senator Raff Ciccone said the public servants’ concerns should be taken seriously.

“Perhaps this parliament should look at how evidence given to committees is used and whether MPs need our own standards for how we describe witness evidence online,” he said in the chamber.

canberra.title: ‘Not enough’: Union members reject ACT Government’s latest pay and conditions offer
canberra.snippet: It’s back to the drawing board for the ACT Government as public servants vote ‘no’ to a 9 per cent pay rise over three ...
canberra.content:
9 September 2026

Start the conversation

Public service union members have rejected the ACT Government’s latest pay and conditions offer. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

It’s back to the drawing board for the ACT Government as public servants vote ‘no’ to a 9 per cent pay rise over three years.

A total of 5928 people (51 per cent of eligible workers) voted on the latest ACT Public Sector Enterprise Agreement bargaining round – the third offer put forward since negotiations began.

Of that, 63 per cent (3741) voted no to the proposed salary increases, which also included a $600 cost-of-living payment if the ACT’s annual CPI reached 3.5 per cent or higher, increasing to $1000 if CPI hit 4 per cent or higher.

New leave conditions and entitlements on the table included expanded access to parental leave for both parents, increasing the cap on personal leave (without the need for evidence) to 10 days, increasing rest relief to a minimum of 10 hours (including travel time between shifts), and introducing a new clause addressing the use of AI in the workplace.

Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) regional secretary Maddy Northam said this confirmed the message union members have pushed all along: “this offer is not enough”.

“This result belongs to every member who took action, stood together and refused to accept a deal that would leave workers worse off,” she said.

“The Barr Government now needs to come back to the table with a fairer offer – one that recognises the value of public sector workers and delivers real improvements on pay, superannuation and flexible work.”

This vote was specifically on the ACTPS Administrative and Related Classifications Enterprise Agreement 2026-2029, which forms the basis of the other enterprise agreements under negotiation.

CPSU members have escalated action in recent months, with sonographers walking off the job to secure better pay.

Ms Northam said protected industrial action would continue.

“We will keep the pressure on until ACT public sector workers have an agreement that does not send them backwards,” she said.

“CPSU members are putting this government on notice. Table a reasonable pay offer or face extensive industrial action across the service.”

The Health Services Union, ASMOF and CFMEU are among other unions that have applied to the Fair Work Commission for protected industrial action.

CFMEU general services officers recently expanded their partial work ban on weekend litter picking to now cover Gungahlin, Belconnen, Braddon and Kippax.

ACT assistant secretary Michael Hiscox previously said workers would keep campaigning until they received a deal that “properly” addressed cost-of-living pressures.

“Prices have risen 3.5 per cent over the year while the government is offering workers 3 per cent,” he said.

“At current inflation, that means a real pay cut. Canberra’s frontline workers don’t deserve to go backwards.”

Public Service Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the rejected offer was a “genuine attempt” to reach a fair and balanced agreement.

“[It contained] a pay rise above the projected rate of inflation over the next three years and substantial improvements in conditions,” she said.

“This result comes at a time when we know workers are facing cost of living pressures and ongoing uncertainty about inflation and interest rates.”

Ms Stephen-Smith said the government had heard the feedback from union members and would continue to negotiate in good faith.

“We’re committed to delivering an outcome for workers while continuing to manage the ACT budget in a responsible way,” she said.

“We understand ACT public servants are also keen to see an outcome sooner rather than later, so we’ll be working quickly on the next steps forward.”

canberra.title: Celebrate Spring away from the Floriade crowds at Parliament House
canberra.snippet: As part of this year’s Floriade celebration, Parliament House is inviting visitors to experience the joy of spring in its sunny cou...
canberra.content:
9 September 2026

Start the conversation

Landscapers have been working around the clock to prepare the Parliament for Spring. Photo: APH.

As part of this year’s Floriade celebration, Parliament House is inviting visitors to experience the joy of spring in its sunny courtyards and enjoy seasonal high teas at the Queen’s Terrace Cafe.

For the next few weeks, visitors can enjoy a guided tour through Parliament’s courtyards, see spaces usually closed to the public, and learn fascinating insights into the landscape architecture and design of the House.

“The Landscape Services team at the Department of Parliamentary Services has worked tirelessly throughout the year to ensure the internal courtyards, formal gardens and native gardens are looking their very best for the Floriade season, creating a stunning display for everyone to enjoy,” Speaker of the House of Representatives Milton Dick said.

An ideal companion to Floriade, this event offers a quieter way to experience spring away from the crowds, with just as much natural beauty in the garden’s pansies, azaleas, cherry and crab apple trees.

“The Spring Courtyards Tour is a feast for the senses, showcasing vibrant displays of colour, fragrant seasonal blooms and a wonderful opportunity to experience these remarkable spaces at their best,” President of the Senate, Senator Sue Lines said.

“The Spring High Tea, inspired by the flavours of the season, includes treats with honey harvested from the Parliament House beehives.”

Treats even include honey from Parliament’s own beehives. Photo: Australian Parliament House.

Visitors can add a refreshment package to their tickets, which includes a fresh scone from Parliament’s pastry chefs and a hot drink of choice from the cafe.

For those looking to elevate their visit, the seasonal high tea experience adds a selection of sweet and savoury treats showcasing Australian produce, inspired by the season. A kid’s high tea is also available.

Tours run from 11 September to 3 October on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, with an accessible tour on 11 and 25 September.

More information on the Spring Courtyards Tour and the Spring High Tea is available on the Australian Parliament House website.

australia.title: Man shot dead in Sydney community centre car park
australia.snippet: NSW police say a vehicle was seen driving away from the scene in Punchbowl in the city’s south-west Get our breaking news email , free ap...
australia.content:
A man has been shot dead in the car park of a Sydney community centre in the city’s south-west.

Emergency services were called to the community centre on Rossmore Avenue in Punchbowl on Wednesday evening after reports of a shooting.

A vehicle was seen driving away from the location after the fatal shooting, NSW police said in a statement.

Paramedics treated the man but he died at the scene. He is yet to be identified, police said.

The fatal shooting comes two days after the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced measures to curb gangland violence in Sydney.

New laws being introduced in the state include new aggravated offences for conspiracy to commit gang-related murder. The maximum penalty will be increased to life imprisonment.

The government has repeatedly denied criminal gangs are “out of control” in the city after the mistaken identity shootings of electrician Joshua Macdonald and Marco Tapia, a 23-year-old biomedical engineering student last week.

Police said neither man had any link to organised crime.

The new laws being introduced in NSW aim to tackle organised crime by giving police more power, including using new interim serious crime prevention orders to restrict people suspected of serious and organised crime. Those would be applied while the state’s supreme court considers the full order.

Children’s indictable offences would include activities linked to organised crime, and public shootings and firebombings would be added to the scheme.

In a statement on Monday, Minns said people who conspire to arrange a gangland murder should face the prospect of “spending the rest of your life behind bars”.

“We want to hit these criminal networks at every point – the people who organise the violence, the people who facilitate it online and the people who ultimately carry it out,” he said.

Police are urging anyone with information about the Punchbowl incident to contact Campsie police station or Crime Stoppers.

australia.title: ‘Costly lemon’ or life-changing laws? Victoria to become first in Australia to offer right to work from home
australia.snippet: The Carroll government has made several amendments to the bill after consulting with business leaders. How will the laws work, and will t...
australia.content:
Australian-first laws that would guarantee workers the right to work from home two days a week are expected to pass the Victorian parliament this week.

The laws were first announced in 2025 by the then premier, Jacinta Allan, just months after Peter Dutton and the Coalition lost the federal election, in part because of his plan to force public servants back into the office full-time.

Despite widespread opposition to the proposal from some of the country’s largest business lobby groups, the equal opportunity amendment (work from home) bill passed parliament’s lower house – with support from the Coalition – in July.

That same week, Ben Carroll toppled Allan as Labor leader. One of his first moves as premier was to pause debate in the upper house to allow for consultation with business leaders – and on Wednesday, the government confirmed several amendments to the bill following these discussions.

Here’s what we know.

australia.title: White Australia party is ‘modern manifestation’ of Nazi movement and should be banned, commonwealth tells high court
australia.snippet: The former National Socialist Network is challenging ban in high court, arguing law breaches implied freedom of political communication G...
australia.content:
The White Australia party is a “modern manifestation” of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi movement and would motivate hate crimes against sections of the country, the high court has heard.

The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio) passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke.

It is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers.

It also argues the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia.

The commonwealth’s lawyer, Brendan Lim, told the court on Wednesday that the group sought to create a political party after anti-hate laws passed in the wake of the Bondi terror attack threatened to disband it.

The hate group listing means that supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitutes a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.

Lim said the group sought “protection” under the guise of creating a political party but remained the same group with the same goals.

The barrister cited a series of examples, including inflammatory rhetoric to encourage communal violence, an alleged physically violent attack by some of its members on Camp Sovereignty in 2025, and past criminal convictions of its leader, Thomas Sewell.

Justice Robert Beech-Jones asked whether the commonwealth believed the group were the “modern manifestation” of Hitler’s Nazi movement. Lim responded: “Yes.”

“There are few legitimate reasons, outside of history books and museum, that warrant the use of Nazi symbols,” Lim said.

Citing a briefing from Asio and public speeches by its director general, Mike Burgess, Lim said the prohibited hate group listing was necessary because the group were security conscious and its operations savvy enough to work within the limits of the law.

“The existence of the group itself is the source of harm,” Lim said.

Lim said stochastic terrorism – the use of media and public discourse to demonise sections of the community – could lead lone wolves or fringe members to commit racially motivated hate crimes.

Lim said the anti-hate laws go “no further than necessary” to remove that harm.

Beech-Jones asked whether the party represented a greater threat to Australia’s nationhood than that of the Communist party in 1950 when prime minister Robert Menzies first banned the party. The ban was overturned the following year as constitutionally invalid.

Lim said the current context was different but both parties represented “great threats” to the country.

Lawyers for the party argued on Tuesday that a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”.

Barrister Shahed Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to outlaw any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation.

Sharify said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision.

Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”.

australia.title: Liberal operative says request to be wired before meeting was ‘silly’ comment, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Jeremy Greenwood tells inquiry he does not remember a plan to release a false ‘mistress photo’ relating to David Elliott Follow our Austr...
australia.content:
A factional figure has denied he requested to be fitted with a wire before a meeting with fellow Liberals and said he can’t recall a plan to have the YouTuber Friendlyjordies run a negative documentary on a New South Wales minister, an inquiry has heard.

Jeremy Greenwood told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Wednesday that a request to be “wire[d] … for sound” before a meeting with other Liberals was a “just a silly comment”.

Icac is investigating the allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from fugitive developer Jean Nassif or his company Toplace in exchange for political outcomes.

They allegedly included the removal of the building commissioner David Chandler and damage to the career of the former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott.

Greenwood and Charles Perrottet, who is a brother of the former premier Dominic Perrottet, have denied taking illegal political donations. Ellis is overseas and is not expected to give evidence during the hearings. Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Greenwood was asked on Wednesday about a message he wrote to Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran ahead of a meeting with Liberal figures, in which he wrote: “Can I get Shane to wire me for sound tomorrow, and you guys pick up the bill?”

Maheswaran replied: “I can give you the equipment, or Shane can”.

Accepting the message referred to a private investigator employed by Toplace, Greenwood said it was a “silly” or “stupid comment”, and he did not believe the meeting took place.

He was asked by the counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC about a message Maheswaran sent to him in which Maheswaran wrote: “Let’s get that material to FriendlyJordies, a one-hour documentary on [Elliott], and then follow it up by releasing the mistress photo”.

Greenwood accepted the message likely referred to Elliott but said he could not recall what material Maheswaran was referring to. The inquiry was previously told that Greenwood and members of conservative factional group the Reformers created a “shit sheet” to discredit Elliott, including an allegation of an extramarital affair which Elliott has strenuously denied and witnesses including Greenwood have accepted is untrue.

Maheswaran, who is named as a person of interest in a separate Icac allegation, and has previously denied any wrongdoing, is expected to appear before the commission.

On Wednesday afternoon, questioning turned to an agreement where Charles Perrottet was remunerated for his advice to Nassif on his developments. The payments were made from lobbying companies controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, to Charles’s wife, Anita Perrottet.

Last week, Charles rejected the suggestion that he or his wife had lied to Icac, after she told the commission that payments to her were for genuine “strategic and marketing advice” she provided, while he said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif and her work.

Greenwood acknowledged the agreement for the first time on Wednesday, saying “Charles’s advice was [of] far more benefit to [lobbying company] Beckington, but Anita’s was far more ongoing”, describing Charles’s advice using “the old analogy about a plumber”.

“You don’t pay them for how they hit the hammer, but knowing where to hit.”

The commission has previously heard there is no written record of advice Anita Perrottet gave to Beckington, which she said took the form of verbal advice. She said advice for Beckington client Greyhound Racing NSW, for which she was paid a $10,000 monthly retainer, included “creating websites … on how to properly humanely treat [dogs]”.

Greenwood on Wednesday said it was normal in the lobbying industry for advice to be verbal. He said he could remember Anita Perrottet coming up with the slogan “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for Greyhound Racing NSW, which he said was now industry policy.

Anita Perrottet told Icac advice provided to Greenwood’s lobbying firm JPG Advisory for an unknown “vaping client” included removing flavours to discourage minors from vaping.

On Wednesday, Greenwood described himself and Ellis, former both parliamentary advisers, as coming from the “Canberra bubble”, saying Anita Perrottet provided a “mum’s perspective”.

“The mum’s perspective is so important. It’s what everybody in politics looks for,” he said.

Dwyer, suggesting it was “absolutely common sense that you shouldn’t have flavours like bubblegum”, said: “You don’t need to pay Anita Perrottet up to $10,000 for a consultancy fee to get a mum’s perspective to come up with that.”

“You’re absolutely right, it’s common sense. Three years ago, it was legal,” Greenwood responded.

‘The Porsche comes in January’

On Monday, Greenwood told the commission about an agreement made in April 2020 with Nassif under which Beckington, controlled by him and Ellis, would be awarded $1m for each of up to five Toplace projects, if they were able to have them fast-tracked.

Following the agreement, the men allegedly discussed whether to buy a Porsche or Ferrari. The inquiry heard on Wednesday that after Greenwood complained about a lack of payment from Toplace, Ellis messaged him in December 2020 that an invoice of $400,000 had been paid.

“Good because the Porsche comes in January and I’m getting worried, but it’s also just really disrespectful from him [Nassif],” responded Greenwood.

In subsequent messages, he described Nassif as a “fuckwit” and said he had told Maheswaran that Nassif was “fucking the relationship”.

Greenwood has said the only written record of the agreement was a note once stored in the back of the Toplace general manager’s phone case. He claimed it contained the names of two of the projects, was folded in half, and was “fuchsia” or “purple-pink” in colour.

Dwyer suggested he had made up the piece of paper, which he accepted he had not mentioned in a preliminary interview with Icac.

Dwyer said: “That’s because it was a recent invention that you came up with on Monday or prior to Monday to explain that arrangement, isn’t it?”

“No, that’s absolutely incorrect,” Greenwood said.

Nassif is scheduled to appear via video link from Lebanon. He withdrew from an appearance last week after providing a medical certificate.

The inquiry continues.

australia.title: Albanese says ABC ‘should do better’ after it revealed his membership of golf club given $6m grant
australia.snippet: Funding from $560m invitation-only scheme prompts calls to make grant rules more transparent Get our new political email , free app or da...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has claimed he did not know he was a member of his local golf club when his government gave it $6m for renovations, accusing the ABC of inappropriate reporting.

The money came from an opaque $560m invitation-only grants scheme to fund projects Labor promised at the 2025 election, largely for Labor-held seats, prompting calls to make grant rules more transparent.

The prime minister had not declared he was an honorary member of the Marrickville Golf Club, which falls in his inner-west Sydney electorate of Grayndler. Albanese told ABC TV on Wednesday the membership was issued by the club 15 years ago without his knowledge.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“I haven’t been in there for years,” Albanese said. “I used to walk my dog along the path, as lots of people do, because it’s a community club.”

The ABC, which first reported the story on Wednesday, said that Albanese’s office had not answered its questions about his membership, or the process by which the Marrickville Golf Club was identified and recommended for the grant. Albanese accused the broadcaster of failing to report the facts.

“The ABC were told information they chose not to publish appropriately,” he said. “The ABC should do better.”

Albanese said the club’s funding was meant to fix issues caused by raw sewerage flowing into the adjacent Cooks River.

“I make no apologies for my electorate being serviced by me as a good local member,” Albanese said

In opposition, Labor claimed the Coalition government unfairly favoured its seats. That controversy, which became known as “sports rorts”, led to then sports minister Bridget McKenzie resigning from cabinet after she failed to disclose membership of a gun club that received funding. An inquiry by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet found she had breached ministerial standards.

Albanese’s electorate received two more grants, for a women’s health centre and a domestic violence shelter.

Eden-Monaro, a New South Wales marginal electorate held by a Labor minister, received eight grants totalling $26.4m, according to analysis of the $560m program by the Centre for Public Integrity (CPI).

Kristy McBain, the minister, told ABC Radio she had listened to local councils’ priorities for new infrastructure then put those forward as potential election commitments that Labor could make.

Crossbench MPs complained that councils in their electorates were not given the opportunity to seek funding from the program. McBain said in response: “I mean, obviously that’s how election commitments work.”

While Albanese and McBain’s electorates received millions of dollars, NSW over all received disproportionately less funding from the program in terms of its population, the CPI found. Queensland also received a disproportionately small amount while Victoria and Tasmania received disproportionately more.

The infrastructure minister, Catherine King, said she had signed off on applications under the program after they had been assessed to show they met value for money.

“That is what happens after every single election,” King said.

The justifications for the grants have not been made public. Thirteen crossbenchers have called for the government reform its grants rules to be transparent about how and why it chose to allocate public money.

The Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie said the existing rules permitting funding for “pet projects” were undermining Australia’s democracy.

“I don’t care how the government spins it,” Lambie said. “Using taxpayer money to buy votes or benefit party followers should be seen as corruption because that’s what it is.”

Additional reporting by AAP

world.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
world.snippet: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems Babies born to mother...
world.content:
Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.

Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.

Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.

Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”

The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.

While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.

“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.

The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

world.title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
world.snippet: US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali...
world.content:
The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.

Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.

The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.

However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.

In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.

He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”

According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”

Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.

Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.

Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.

Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.

According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.

Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.

That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.

In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.

During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.

Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.

The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.

Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.

“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.

“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.

“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

world.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
world.snippet: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive hea...
world.content:
Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.

This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

world.title: Egyptian TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death for drug crime
world.snippet: Sarah Khalifa, 39, charged with forming organised criminal gang to manufacture and traffic drugs An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known...
world.content:
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.

The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.

The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.

The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.

The verdict is subject to appeal.

Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

According to the state-run Akhbar el-Yom newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”.

Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.

The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.

Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.

According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

world.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
world.snippet: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland The United Nations has ...
world.content:
The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.

In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design.

At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions.

UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.

Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”.

Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.”

The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard.

Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.

“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.

On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution.

Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.

Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.

One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.

Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.

Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.

He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”

Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.

Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”

He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”
